extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator; educated general public interested in morals, manners, and satire
extracted.subtask_description: Short, moralizing satirical essays that expose vice and folly in social behaviour (patronage, family relations, lotteries, court levées) using letters, anecdotes, and humorous portraits. Aimed at public instruction and entertainment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admiration should track virtue, not circumstance
rubrics_metrics.description: “still more ridiculous, is, that it is usually given for Circumstances which are foreign to the Persons admired. ... The Application only, and not the Possession, makes those outward things honourable.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admiration and praise ought to be directed to the person's virtue or merit rather than to accidental outward circumstances (wealth, power) that may be transferred; criticizes those who admire people for possessions rather than character. Anti‑pattern: applauding someone solely because they hold office or money.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid dedicating works to ignorant patrons
rubrics_metrics.description: “Dedications to ignorant Men are as absurd as any of the Speeches of Bulfinch in the Droll: Such an Address one is apt to translate into other Words; ... the Panegyrick generally implies no more than if the Author should say to the Patron; My very good Lord, You and I can never understand one another, therefore I humbly desire we may be intimate Friends for the future.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Addresses or dedications made to patrons who do not share the author's taste or learning are ridiculous and invite ridicule; they make the panegyric seem insincere and absurd. Example/anti‑pattern: flattering an ignorant wealthy patron in hopes of preferment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Praise from unworthy sources is worthless
rubrics_metrics.description: “He that commends another engages so much of his own Reputation as he gives to that Person commended; and he that has nothing laudable in himself is not of Ability to be such a Surety.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A person's reputation is partly mortgaged by the people who praise them; endorsements from those without virtue or merit cannot truly enhance one's character. Use this to judge the value of public praise. Example: Phocion's reaction to popular acclamation—wise men should question applause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use exposure of deformity to deter imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: “I have exposed this Picture of an unnatural Father with the same Intention, that its Deformity may deter others from its Resemblance.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satirical portraits of extreme vice or folly should be presented clearly so their deformity deters readers from copying them. Method: place an exaggerated negative example before readers so the absurdity serves as moral instruction. Anti‑pattern: ambiguous satire that fails to signal the vice being condemned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not blindly side with children in family controversies
rubrics_metrics.description: “I must not however engage my self blindly on the Side of the Son ... To go about railing at his Father, and to find no other Place but the Outside of his Letter to tell him that Might overcomes Right, ... we may at least allow that the Father will do very well in endeavouring to better his Judgment, and give him a greater Sense of his Duty.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When discussing disputes between parents and children, examine both parties; do not assume filial innocence. Moral commentary should weigh actions on both sides and avoid encouraging disobedience without scrutiny. Use concrete details of conduct to form judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parental obligations and filial duty as social foundation
rubrics_metrics.description: “The Obligations on that Side can never be acquitted, and I think it is one of the greatest Reflections upon Human Nature that Parental Instinct should be a stronger Motive to Love than Filial Gratitude ... The Obedience of Children to their Parents is the Basis of all Government.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat parental care and filial obedience as primary social duties; in moral or political argument use parental obligation as a foundation for social order. Example/appeal to foreign customs (Chinese, Persian) to illustrate the gravity of filial impiety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use vivid epistolary voices to expose hypocrisy and social vice
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper prints letters from varied voices (a father’s brutal billet, letters from women of the town, and the lottery dreamer) to present different social perspectives and follies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ first‑person letters and distinct character voices to reveal hypocrisy, vice, and absurdities in society; this variety supplies material for humour and moral reflection. Example: letters from prostitutes reveal social double standards; anti‑pattern: vague generalization without concrete voices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satirize caprice and superstition in choices
rubrics_metrics.description: “These Principles of Election are the Pastimes and Extravagancies of Human Reason ... Caprice very often acts in the Place of Reason ... some are pleased to find their own Age in their Number; some ... because it is the same Number that succeeded in the last Lottery.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expose and ridicule the irrational motives people use in decisions (lottery number choices, belief in lucky numbers); contrast caprice with reason to produce comic effect and moral lesson. Example: mock fortune‑tellers who could exploit lotteries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Live within your possessions; avoid living on expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: “It should be an indispensable Rule in Life, to contract our Desires to our present Condition ... We live up to our Expectations, not to our Possessions ... The Man who lives by Hope will die by Hunger.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use moral aphorisms and illustrative anecdotes to counsel prudence: do not spend as if contingent future gains are certain. Anti‑pattern: romantic generosity and senseless ostentation that end in ruin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good habits, not wealth, shape progeny
rubrics_metrics.description: “Good Habits are what will certainly improve a Man's Fortune and Reputation; but on the other side, Affluence of Fortune will not as probably produce good Affections of the Mind.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argue that industry, probity, valour, and justice—habits and education—are what parents can and should bequeath to children; wealth alone does not guarantee virtue. Use comparisons of families (Cornelii vs Ruricola’s heir) as evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promote unreserved correspondence between father and son
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is the most beautiful Object the Eyes of Man can behold, to see a Man of Worth and his Son live in an entire unreserved Correspondence. The mutual Kindness and Affection ... is as sacred as Friendship, as pleasurable as Love, and as joyful as Religion.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocate affability, example, and close familiar conduct from parents to children rather than severity; show benefits (comfort in old age, perpetuation of reputation). Anti‑pattern: distant, severe parenting which breeds degeneracy in heirs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Levée behaviour and patron–client theatre
rubrics_metrics.description: “For the Benefit of these ... it would not methinks be amiss to give an Account of that Market for Preferment, a great Man's Levée. ... the close Minister is buttoned up, and the brave Officer open‑breasted ... the Business of a Levée is to receive the Acknowledgments of a Multitude ... he has something to say to every Man there, and that so suitable to his Capacity.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe the social choreography of court levées as a spectacle: patrons should appear affable and give opportunities to clients to show themselves; clients cultivate a polite, servile demeanour. Use comic detail (half‑dressed officers, whispering valet) to lampoon the pretensions of both sides. Practical note: in satire, detail the ritual to expose its emptiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technique: employ concrete anecdote and exaggeration for humour
rubrics_metrics.description: Throughout the papers the author uses extreme letters (cruel father, bawdy women), vivid anecdotes (lottery dreamer, Doctor's bells), and caricatured scenes to make moral points and produce laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For effective satirical humour, present concrete, specific examples and amplify absurd features rather than argue abstractly. Expose folly by staging it; the more particular and oddly detailed, the clearer the ridicule. Anti‑pattern: abstract condemnation without memorable particulars.
